notice: RN bank batch 84: Management of Care and Safety: competing priorities, supervision, accountability, ethics and exposure safety. Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026. See REVIEW-LOG.md. Also carries the bank-wide catalog (catalog.py): the RN Question Bank and every curated test set.

subtopics.name: Discharge planning and continuity of care

questions.stem: At 0700 the nurse reviews new laboratory results for four clients on a medical unit. Which result should the nurse act on first?

options.text: Glucose 324 mg/dL in a client with type 2 diabetes who is alert, has no ketones and is due a scheduled insulin dose at 0730
Potassium 6.2 mEq/L in a client with chronic kidney disease whose telemetry now shows tall, peaked T waves
Hemoglobin 7.9 g/dL in a client with known chronic anemia whose value was 8.0 yesterday and who has no symptoms
Sodium 131 mEq/L in a client taking hydrochlorothiazide who is alert and oriented and was 132 mEq/L two days ago

rationale.correct: Act first on the result that threatens life now: an electrolyte value with ECG changes outranks stable or chronic abnormalities.

perOption.a: High glucose needs correction, but the client is stable and the scheduled insulin is about to be given.
perOption.b: Hyperkalemia with ECG changes can progress to a fatal dysrhythmia within minutes and needs immediate treatment.
perOption.c: A stable, chronic value without symptoms can be reported after the urgent problem.
perOption.d: Mild, stable hyponatremia without neurological changes is not urgent.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Laboratory reference ranges as used in common NCLEX review texts; follow the facility's ranges
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Prioritize laboratory results using clinical context.

questions.stem: The nurse delegates turning and repositioning to an assistive personnel (AP) for a client who had a posterior-approach total hip replacement yesterday. Which instruction is most important to give the AP?

options.text: Use a lift sheet and two people so the client's skin does not shear on the sheets
Keep the abduction pillow between the legs, and report a leg that looks shorter or turned outward
Turn the client at 2-hour intervals and record each new position on the turning schedule kept at the bedside
Offer the bedpan before each turn so that the client does not need to be moved twice within a short period

rationale.correct: When delegating, give the instruction that targets the client's most serious specific risk and states exactly what to report.

perOption.a: Preventing shear matters, but the most specific danger after posterior hip replacement is dislocation.
perOption.b: Hip dislocation is the key risk; the AP must keep the legs abducted and know which signs to report at once.
perOption.c: Timing and charting are routine; they do not address the most serious risk of this surgery.
perOption.d: This is helpful but does not prevent the most serious complication.

questions.stem: The charge nurse is assigning clients on a medical unit. Which 2 clients should be assigned to the most experienced RN?

options.text: A client with a new tracheostomy who needs frequent suctioning and has had two episodes of desaturation this morning
A client with stable cellulitis who is receiving IV antibiotics and is walking independently
A client with a GI bleed who received one unit of blood and whose heart rate is rising again
A client with type 2 diabetes who is being discharged today after teaching was completed yesterday
A client with chronic back pain who needs scheduled oral analgesics and help with walking

rationale.correct: Give the most complex and unstable clients to the most experienced nurse; stable, predictable clients can go to others.

perOption.a: Unstable airway status needs the strongest assessment and rapid response skills.
perOption.b: Stable, predictable care can be given by a less experienced nurse.
perOption.c: Possible ongoing bleeding needs close, skilled monitoring.
perOption.d: Discharge with completed teaching is predictable.
perOption.e: Predictable care that does not need the most experienced nurse.

questions.educationalObjective: Match client acuity to nurse experience.

questions.stem: While eating lunch, a client suddenly grabs at their throat. The client is coughing forcefully and can say, "It went down the wrong way." The face is red but the lips are pink. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give abdominal thrusts right away and keep going until the piece of food comes out
Encourage coughing and stay close, ready to act if the cough weakens
Give the client a glass of water to help wash the food down
Sweep the back of the throat with a gloved finger to pull out the piece of food

rationale.correct: With a mild airway obstruction (effective cough, can speak), encourage coughing and watch closely; use thrusts only if the client cannot cough, speak or breathe.

perOption.a: Thrusts are for a severe obstruction when the client cannot cough, speak or breathe.
perOption.b: A forceful cough and speech show a partial obstruction with good air exchange; coughing is the best way to clear it.
perOption.c: Fluids can worsen choking or cause aspiration.
perOption.d: Blind finger sweeps can push the object deeper.

references: American Heart Association Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to a partial airway obstruction.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing four clients at the start of a shift. For each client, indicate when the nurse should act.

rows.text: Client 2 days after a colectomy whose wound edges have separated with pink tissue showing through
Client with pneumonia whose temperature is 38.3 °C (101 °F) and whose next antibiotic dose is due in 45 minutes
Client with heart failure who asks for help ordering a low-sodium lunch
Client with diabetes who is shaky and sweating with a glucose of 58 mg/dL

rationale.correct: Act now on threats to life or rapid deterioration; address expected problems within the hour; routine needs can follow.

perOption.r1:c1: Dehiscence can progress to evisceration; it needs covering with moist sterile dressing and reporting now.
perOption.r2:c1: Fever is expected and the client is stable.
perOption.r2:c2: Give an antipyretic and continue antibiotics as scheduled.
perOption.r2:c3: A fever still needs attention this hour.
perOption.r4:c2: Waiting could lead to loss of consciousness.

questions.stem: A client with moderate Alzheimer's disease needs a PEG tube. The client's daughter is the durable power of attorney for health care and has signed the consent. When the nurse prepares the client, the client pulls away and says, "No! Don't touch me!" What should the nurse do?

options.text: Proceed, since the daughter is the legal decision-maker and has already consented
Stop, calm the client and tell the provider and daughter about the objection
Ask security staff to hold the client still so that the procedure can start on time as scheduled
Cancel the procedure permanently, since the client has clearly refused it

rationale.correct: Even when a substitute decision-maker has consented, a client's objection or distress is respected, reported and reviewed before care proceeds.

perOption.a: The agent's consent is valid, but the client's distress must be addressed and the team informed before going ahead.
perOption.b: The client's distress and objection must be respected and reviewed with the agent and provider, even when the agent has consented.
perOption.c: Physically forcing care on a frightened client is not acceptable.
perOption.d: A client without capacity cannot make the final decision, but the objection must be reviewed rather than ignored or treated as final.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to the objection of a client who lacks capacity.

questions.stem: While reviewing records, the nurse notices that a coworker has charted full assessments for three clients whom the coworker did not visit during the shift. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Ignore it, since the coworker is experienced and the clients seem fine
Report the concern to the charge nurse or nurse manager according to policy
Correct the coworker's entries in the record so they show what really happened
Post a reminder in the staff break room about accurate charting for everyone

rationale.correct: Falsifying documentation is a serious violation; report it through the chain of command and do not change another person's entries.

perOption.a: False documentation endangers clients and is a legal and ethical violation.
perOption.b: Falsified documentation must be reported through the chain of command so it can be investigated.
perOption.c: Nurses cannot alter another person's documentation.
perOption.d: A general reminder does not address a specific, serious violation.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.stem: A client with advanced bone cancer says, "I want you to give me enough morphine to end this. Please help me die." Medical aid in dying is not legal in this state. What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "I can't do that, and it's against the law, so let's not talk about it."
"Tell me more about what is making things so hard right now, including your pain."
"I'll ask the provider to increase your morphine so that you can sleep through most of this."
"Many people feel this way, and it usually passes after a few days of rest."

rationale.correct: When a client asks for help to die, explore the request, assess pain, depression and suicide risk, and involve the palliative team; never take part in ending life where it is illegal.

perOption.a: This closes the conversation and leaves the client's suffering unaddressed.
perOption.b: Requests to die often reflect uncontrolled pain, depression or fear; exploring them lets the team treat the cause and assess safety.
perOption.c: This avoids the request and suggests sedation as an answer.
perOption.d: This minimizes the client's distress.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to a request to hasten death.

questions.stem: In a crowded hospital elevator, the nurse hears two staff members discussing a client's new cancer diagnosis by name. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Say nothing in the elevator and report both staff members anonymously later in the day
Quietly remind them they can be overheard and suggest talking in private
Join the conversation to make sure the facts about the client that they share are correct
Tell the other people in the elevator to forget what they heard

rationale.correct: Protect privacy by stopping public discussion of clients right away, then follow facility policy for reporting.

perOption.a: The breach is ongoing; a quiet word now stops it.
perOption.b: Stopping the breach right away protects the client; follow-up reporting may also be needed.
perOption.c: This adds to the breach.
perOption.d: This draws attention to the breach without stopping it.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.stem: A 79-year-old client who lives alone is being discharged on warfarin for new atrial fibrillation. The client has macular degeneration and cannot read the print on pill bottles. Which plan best supports safe medication use at home?

options.text: Give the client a large-print written schedule and ask them to call with questions
Arrange home health nursing, a pre-filled pill organizer and an INR check this week
Ask a friendly neighbor to read the labels each day and remind the client to take the warfarin
Ask the provider to switch the client to a drug that does not need to be taken daily

rationale.correct: Plan discharge around the client's specific barrier and the risks of the drug: support administration and arrange early monitoring for high-alert medications.

perOption.a: Large print helps but may still be hard to read, and it does not ensure INR monitoring.
perOption.b: Home health can fill an organizer and monitor the client, and an early INR check makes warfarin safer.
perOption.c: An informal helper may not be reliable for a high-alert drug.
perOption.d: Anticoagulants are taken daily; this does not solve the vision problem.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.educationalObjective: Plan safe discharge for a client with a high-alert drug and impaired vision.

questions.stem: A night nurse on a medical unit finishes the 0700 bedside handoff with these four clients still waiting. Rank the clients from the one the nurse should see first to the one who can wait longest.

items.text: A client 1 day after surgery who reports new calf pain and swelling
A client being discharged today who wants to review the medication list
A client with diabetes due for a scheduled insulin dose with breakfast
A client with COPD who is now drowsy and difficult to arouse, with SpO2 85% on 4 L/min

rationale.correct: Rank by threat: airway and breathing first, then possible complications, then timed medications, then routine teaching.

perOption.a: Decreasing consciousness with hypoxemia suggests CO2 narcosis and airway risk.
perOption.b: Possible DVT needs assessment and reporting soon.
perOption.c: Timed medication with the meal.
perOption.d: Discharge teaching is important but least urgent.

questions.stem: A client with schizophrenia has been admitted four times this year after stopping medication. The client is unhoused and has no phone. Which community resource best fits this client's needs?

options.text: A once-a-month outpatient psychiatry appointment at the hospital clinic
An assertive community treatment (ACT) team that comes to the client
A printed list of local shelters and food banks given to the client at discharge
A peer support group that meets once a week at a church across town

rationale.correct: Assertive community treatment provides intensive, mobile, team-based care for people with serious mental illness who struggle with traditional services.

perOption.a: Monthly clinic visits do not reach a client without housing or a phone.
perOption.b: ACT teams bring medication, housing help and support to clients where they are, reducing readmissions.
perOption.c: A list alone rarely leads to stable housing or treatment.
perOption.d: Support groups help, but they do not provide the intensive services this client needs.

questions.educationalObjective: Choose a community resource for serious mental illness.

questions.stem: A nurse notices that staff on the unit routinely put normal saline into tracheostomy tubes before suctioning, which the nurse learned is no longer recommended. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Stop instilling saline in the nurse's own practice and say nothing to others
Review current evidence and take it to the practice council or educator
Tell the staff in the hallway that they have been doing the procedure wrong for years
Write a new unit policy on suctioning and post it in the clean utility room

rationale.correct: To change practice, gather current evidence and bring it through the unit's practice council, educator or quality process.

perOption.a: Changing only personal practice leaves other clients exposed to the outdated method.
perOption.b: Evidence-based practice changes go through the unit's quality or practice structures.
perOption.c: Public criticism is unprofessional and unlikely to change practice.
perOption.d: Individual staff do not write policy; changes go through the proper process.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with heart failure uses a home telemonitoring scale that sends daily weights to the clinic. This morning's weight is 2.1 kg (4.6 lb) higher than yesterday's. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Wait for tomorrow's weight to see whether the gain is a measurement error
Call the client to ask about breathlessness, swelling and diet
Tell the client by text message to double tomorrow's dose of furosemide
Send an ambulance to the client's home right away so they can be assessed in the emergency department

rationale.correct: Remote monitoring data trigger assessment: contact the client, assess symptoms and causes, then follow protocol or notify the provider.

perOption.a: A rapid gain suggests fluid retention; waiting delays treatment.
perOption.b: The nurse first assesses the client's symptoms and possible causes before deciding on next steps with the provider.
perOption.c: Nurses do not change doses without a prescription.
perOption.d: An ambulance may be needed if the client is in distress, but first the nurse assesses the situation.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing a new client's medication prescriptions. Highlight the prescriptions the nurse should clarify with the prescriber before giving them.

segments.text: Metoprolol tartrate 25 mg by mouth twice daily.
Morphine 2 to 10 mg IV every 2 hours as needed for pain
Acetaminophen 650 mg by mouth every 6 hours as needed for fever
Docusate 100 mg by mouth twice daily

rationale.correct: Clarify prescriptions with unsafe dose ranges, do-not-use abbreviations or missing route, dose or frequency before giving them.

perOption.s2: Very wide dose ranges without criteria are unsafe and need clarification.
perOption.s4: "U" is on the do-not-use list because it can be misread as 0 or 4.
perOption.s8: The route and frequency are missing.

questions.stem: A new assistive personnel (AP) tells the nurse, "I inserted urinary catheters all the time at my last job. Want me to do the one for room 8?" The facility's AP job description does not include catheter insertion. What should the nurse say?

options.text: "Sure, since you have experience, go ahead and let me know when it's done."
"Thanks, but that isn't part of the AP role at this hospital, so I'll do it."
"Go ahead, but I'll watch you this one time to make sure you do it right."
"Ask the charge nurse whether it's OK, and do it if they say yes."

rationale.correct: Delegate only tasks within the delegatee's job description and facility policy, even if they have done them elsewhere.

perOption.a: Delegation must follow the facility's job description, regardless of past experience.
perOption.b: Tasks can be delegated only when they are within the delegatee's role at this facility.
perOption.c: Supervision does not make a task within scope if the role does not include it.
perOption.d: The RN delegating the task is responsible for following the job description.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Apply delegation rules to scope of role.

questions.stem: A client signs the discharge instructions quickly, then quietly asks the nurse's AP what "take twice daily with food" means. The nurse suspects limited health literacy. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Read the instructions aloud again more slowly and have the client sign once more
Review key points in plain language and have the client explain them back
Ask the client whether they have trouble reading in front of the family
Give the client more detailed written handouts to read at home

rationale.correct: Use plain language, focus on key points and use teach-back with every client, since limited health literacy is common and often hidden.

perOption.a: Re-reading does not confirm understanding.
perOption.b: Plain language and teach-back confirm understanding without shaming the client.
perOption.c: Asking publicly can embarrass the client.
perOption.d: More text is less helpful for limited literacy.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.educationalObjective: Teach a client with limited health literacy.

questions.stem: Which situations should the nurse report through the facility's incident reporting system? Select all that apply.

options.text: A client receives the wrong dose of a medication
A client refuses a scheduled walk in the hallway after lunch
An IV pump delivers the wrong rate because of a fault
A visitor faints and hits their head in the hallway
A client's blood pressure is higher than usual before breakfast
A client asks the team to arrange a second opinion

rationale.correct: Incident reports cover errors, equipment failures and injuries to clients, visitors or staff; clinical findings and client choices go in the record.

perOption.a: Medication errors are reported.
perOption.b: This is documented in the record, not an incident.
perOption.c: Equipment failures are reported.
perOption.d: Injuries to visitors are reported.
perOption.e: This is a clinical finding to report to the provider.
perOption.f: This is a client right, not an incident.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify events to report as incidents.

questions.stem: A client is being transferred by ambulance from the hospital to a skilled nursing facility. Who is responsible for giving report to the receiving facility?

options.text: The ambulance crew, since they will deliver the client and the papers
The sending nurse, who gives report directly to the receiving nurse
The client's family, who can describe how the client has been doing over the past week
No one, because the written discharge summary sent with the client is enough for the facility

rationale.correct: The sending nurse gives a direct handoff to the receiving nurse at transitions of care, supported by written records.

perOption.a: Transport staff are not responsible for clinical handoff.
perOption.b: A nurse-to-nurse handoff transfers responsibility and lets the receiving nurse ask questions.
perOption.c: Family input is valuable, but the clinical handoff is a nursing responsibility.
perOption.d: Written summaries do not replace a direct handoff.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Hand off care at a facility transfer.

questions.stem: Only one private room is available on a medical unit. Two new clients need contact precautions: one with MRSA in the sputum who is coughing but continent, and one with Clostridioides difficile who is having frequent incontinent stools. Which client should get the private room?

options.text: The client with MRSA, since coughing spreads organisms more widely than stool
The client with C. difficile, since incontinent stool spreads spores widely
Neither client, because both can share a room on contact precautions
The client who was admitted to the unit first, to keep the room assignment process fair

rationale.correct: When private rooms are limited, give priority to clients whose infections are most likely to contaminate the environment, such as incontinent C. difficile.

perOption.a: MRSA in sputum spreads by contact and droplets, but a continent client with C. difficile is the greater environmental risk here.
perOption.b: Incontinent clients with C. difficile shed spores widely; spores survive on surfaces for months.
perOption.c: Clients with different organisms should not share a room.
perOption.d: Room placement is based on transmission risk, not order of admission.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A nurse is stuck with a hollow needle used to draw blood from a client known to have HIV with a detectable viral load. After washing the site and reporting the injury, what should happen next?

options.text: Wait 6 weeks and then test for HIV antibodies before starting any treatment
Start post-exposure prophylaxis as soon as possible, ideally within 2 hours
Take a single dose of an antibiotic to prevent infection from the needle
Test the client's blood again and decide on treatment after the result

rationale.correct: After a high-risk HIV exposure, start post-exposure prophylaxis as soon as possible (ideally within 2 hours, no later than 72 hours) and arrange follow-up testing.

perOption.a: Waiting misses the window for post-exposure prophylaxis.
perOption.b: PEP is most effective when started within hours and no later than 72 hours after exposure.
perOption.c: Antibiotics do not prevent HIV.
perOption.d: The client's status is known; PEP should not wait.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance

questions.educationalObjective: Act after an HIV needlestick exposure.

questions.stem: A client is placed in physical restraints at 0200 for violent behavior that endangers others, under an emergency order. Which requirement must be met within 1 hour?

options.text: A face-to-face evaluation of the client by a qualified provider or trained RN
Removal of the restraints at the 1-hour mark regardless of the client's behavior
Written consent from the client's family for the use of the restraint
Transfer of the client from the restraints to a locked seclusion room

rationale.correct: Violent-behavior restraint needs an order, a face-to-face evaluation within 1 hour, continuous monitoring and release as soon as safe.

perOption.a: For restraint used for violent behavior, a face-to-face evaluation within 1 hour is required.
perOption.b: Restraints are removed as soon as it is safe, not at a fixed time.
perOption.c: Family consent is not required for emergency restraint.
perOption.d: Seclusion is a separate intervention and not a requirement.

questions.stem: Which practices help prevent wrong-client errors? Select all that apply.

options.text: Using two identifiers, such as name and date of birth, before care
Using the room number as one of the identifiers
Labeling specimens at the bedside in front of the client
Scanning the client's wristband before giving medications
Asking "Are you Mr. Jones?" and waiting for a yes
Reading back verbal and telephone orders

rationale.correct: Prevent wrong-client errors with two identifiers stated by the client, bedside labeling, barcode scanning and read-back.

perOption.a: Two identifiers confirm the right client.
perOption.b: Clients change rooms; room numbers are not identifiers.
perOption.c: Labeling away from the client causes mix-ups.
perOption.d: Barcode scanning adds a check.
perOption.e: Clients may agree without hearing; they should state their name.

questions.stem: The nurse is moving a client up in bed with a coworker. Which action protects the nurse's back?

options.text: Raise the bed to waist height and use a slide sheet
Keep the bed low and bend at the waist to reach the client
Lift the client by pulling under the arms
Twist the trunk while pulling so that the client can be moved up faster

rationale.correct: Safe handling: work at waist height, use friction-reducing devices, keep a wide base and avoid twisting.

perOption.a: Working at waist height with a slide sheet reduces strain on the back.
perOption.b: Bending at the waist strains the back.
perOption.c: Pulling under the arms injures the client and the nurse.
perOption.d: Twisting while lifting injures the back.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: During a heat wave, a public cooling center asks a nurse to check on visitors. Which visitor is at greatest risk of heat-related illness?

options.text: A 30-year-old who runs daily and drinks water throughout the day
An 84-year-old living alone without air conditioning who takes furosemide
A 45-year-old who works in an air-conditioned office and drinks iced coffee
A 20-year-old college student who spent the whole morning swimming laps in an outdoor pool

rationale.correct: Older adults, people living alone without air conditioning and those taking diuretics, anticholinergics or antipsychotics are at highest risk in heat waves.

perOption.a: Fit, well-hydrated adults are at lower risk.
perOption.b: Older age, living alone, no air conditioning and a diuretic all impair the body's ability to stay cool and hydrated.
perOption.c: Working in air conditioning lowers risk.
perOption.d: Pool water cools the body; risk is low.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

testSets.title: NCLEX-RN adaptive exam
testSets.description: Works like the real NCLEX-RN: each question depends on your answers so far, and the exam stops once your result is clear, after 85 to 150 questions. Choose timed (5 hours) or untimed. No going back; answers and rationales at the end. The questions are being rewritten to real NCLEX difficulty and recalibrated, so treat your result as a practice estimate.
